key_insight: Adapting π₀.₅ to robotic chess benefits from more demonstrations and training updates in simulation, while partial real-robot results suggest simulation pretraining helps most when real data is scarce.
engineering_relevance: Simulation pretraining and a short learning-rate cool-down are practical levers for VLA adaptation, but checkpoint selection should rely on task success rather than validation loss or action error.
method: Fine-tune π₀.₅ to move a chess king between named squares using an SO-101 arm.
Vary dataset sizes and update budgets using teleoperated and randomized scripted-expert demonstrations.
Test rollout-based adaptation methods against plain behavior cloning.
evidence_signal: Real-arm experiments used up to 256 demonstrations and evaluated 10 policies over 25 trials each; in simulation, a short learning-rate cool-down added up to 31 percentage points in success rate.
watch_item: Real-robot findings are partial and task-specific; rollout-based methods showed no measurable improvement over behavior cloning in this setting.
paper_title: VLA Adaptation with Real and Simulated Data: A Case Study on Robotic Chess
